title: Write It Down
setting: an ice rink's night plant room

post.author: u/night_ice_hjordis
post.title: I keep the ice at a town rink overnight. The controller says both compressors started at 03:00. The ice says they never ran.

blocks.text: I'm Hjordis, night ice technician at our town's ice rink. I keep the ice at -5 °C for junior hockey practice, 06:00 every weekday. I work in the rink building, on its own electricity supply. It stayed lit all night.

Two compressors keep the ice cold: each is a machine with a big electric motor that chills a liquid; pumps push that liquid through pipes under the ice. Ours sit in the plant room, the machinery room: a brick building across the yard on its own supply.

Electricity is counted in amps: how much flows at once, like litres a second through a pipe. A compressor start goes in steps: the motor pulls 120 amps for its first 5 seconds while it gets up to speed, then settles at 40 amps while it runs. At night the plant room's lights and pumps draw 30 amps.

All of it comes through one main fuse, rated 200 amps: a thick wire in a sealed box where the supply comes in. If more than 200 amps flow for a full second, the wire melts and everything behind it stops. Only the electricity supplier can fit a new one.

The compressors are started by the controller, a grey box in the rink office that switches machines on and off by the clock. Its timetable is called the schedule. Every night the compressors rest from 01:00 to 03:00; the pumps keep the chilled liquid moving, and the ice holds at -5 °C. At 03:00 they start again.

A schedule change goes in steps: you open the schedule on the controller, change a time, type a note saying why, and save. The controller writes it in its change log and follows the new times from that night. Each line of its log is a time, then what happened:

Wed 14 Oct 19:06     contractor: start B 03:02:00 -> 03:00:00
                     note: two start times 2 minutes apart, no reason found, merged for simplicity
Thu 15 Oct 03:00:00  start A sent. start B sent.
Thu 15 Oct 04:30:00  ALARM: ice -1.0 °C. Text sent to night phone.

The contractor serviced the compressors on Wednesday evening and tidied the schedule before leaving. The controller also reads a thermometer in the ice, and its alarm texts my phone when the ice reaches -1 °C. Its half-hourly readings:
At 04:30 I crossed the yard by torch. The plant room was dark and silent: no lights, no pumps, no hum. Nothing in there reports a blown fuse. Only the ice is watched.
The controller said both had started. The ice said nothing had.

I rang the supplier; their engineer fitted a new fuse before dawn, but the ice was soft and practice was cancelled. In the morning I rang old Tamsworth, the rink's engineer before me, retired last December. In January 2024, when these two compressors were fitted, the fuse blew on their first night. He moved B to two minutes after A, and wrote why in the staff chat. That chat tool was switched off this June, history and all.

blocks.label: plant_room_night.png

diagram.aria: Thursday 15 October 2026, 02:30 to 04:40. The controller shows both compressors started from 03:00:00 onwards. The compressors themselves rest until 03:00 and are stopped from 03:00:01. The plant room's power is on until 03:00:01, then the fuse is blown. The ice is green until 03:00, amber from 03:00 to 04:30, red from 04:30. Markers: 03:00:00 both start, 270 amps; 04:30 the alarm at -1.0 °C.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from the controller's log, the ice readings and my sums, Thursday 15 October 2026. The controller shows both compressors started at 03:00:00. That second they drew 120 + 120 + 30 = 270 amps; the 200-amp main fuse blew at 03:00:01 and the plant room went dark, pumps and all. The ice warmed from -5.0 °C at 03:00 to -1.0 °C at 04:30, when the alarm texted me.

blocks.text: Nobody here knew. The contractor looked for a reason and found none. What should we change before the next person tidies the schedule?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Two sums first. Each start is 120 amps for 5 seconds, on top of your 30. The old way, A at 03:00 and B at 03:02, what was the most the plant room ever drew? And last night, both at 03:00:00? Then a question about where reasons live. Some teams keep a decision record: one short page for one decision, saying what was decided, why, and what it costs. Tamsworth's two minutes was a decision. Where was its reason last night?

replies.author: u/night_ice_hjordis
replies.text: The old way: 150 at 03:00, then 40 + 120 + 30 = 190 at 03:02. Last night: 120 + 120 + 30 = 270 at 03:00:00. His reason was in a chat thread nobody can open any more.

comments.author: u/bigger_fuse_diarmuid
comments.text: Paperwork never kept a compressor running. Your fuse is simply too small for your plant. Get a bigger fuse and stop worrying: then it doesn't matter when anything starts or who tidies what, and nobody has to remember anything.

replies.author: u/night_ice_hjordis
replies.text: The fuse belongs to the electricity supplier. I'd have to ask them.

comments.author: u/hard_stop_gwladys
comments.text: Notes get lost; machines don't forget. Our bakery's two ovens can't heat up together, because their controller has a guard: a rule built into it that refuses any timetable starting both within a minute. Ask your controller's maker for the same. Then nobody can save that schedule again.

reply.prompt: The next tidy will come. What should the rink change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Stop outside contractors from changing the schedule, so only rink staff can touch it.
options.part2: From Monday 19 October only rink staff could change the schedule; the contractor's access to the controller was removed. In January the new day technician, tidying the controller before the town's tournament, found two start times 2 minutes apart, no note, no reason, and merged them, just as the contractor had. In the sim the merge draws 270 amps at 03:00:00 whoever saves it, and the fuse blows at 03:00:01. The alarm texted me at 04:30, at -1.0 °C, and I crossed the yard to a dark plant room for the second time.
options.senior: Who may change a setting matters, but the problem here was what the person knew, not who they were. A careful member of staff with no reason in front of them does what the contractor did: a gap with no explanation looks like a mistake. Nygard's warning fits: without the reason, the next person can only blindly accept a decision or blindly change it. Narrowing the circle of people keeps the knowledge in fewer heads; it does not put it anywhere.

options.text: Ask the electricity supplier for a bigger main fuse, so both compressors can start at once.
options.part2: On Friday 16 October I rang the supplier. Their engineer came the next week and explained: the fuse is theirs, sized to the cable from the street, and a bigger one means a new cable, on their timetable, not ours. In the sim a 300-amp fuse would hold the merge: 270 at 03:00:00, and the ice stays at -5.0 °C. Until the cable comes the fuse is 200, and the merged schedule blows it at 03:00:01. And even with 300, nothing would tell the next person that only 30 amps are left to spare.
options.senior: A bigger fuse removes this one limit, if the supplier agrees and the cable allows, and that is their call, on their timetable. It also hides the reason: the 2-minute gap becomes a habit nobody can explain, and the margin, 270 against 300, is written nowhere, so the next machine added to the plant room uses it up unseen. Changing a limit is a fine decision when it is made on purpose and written down; as a way to stop worrying, it trades one lost reason for another.

options.text: Write each decision down beside the schedule, and check every change against it.
options.part2: On Friday 16 October I wrote the rink's first decision record, DR-1, and pinned it beside the controller, with a copy in the schedule's notes: "Never start both compressors within 2 minutes. Why: each start draws 120 amps for 5 seconds, the lights and pumps draw 30, and the main fuse is 200; two starts together draw 270 and blow it. What it costs: B starts 2 minutes later. A gap of 5 seconds would hold; 2 minutes is margin. Look again if the fuse or the night load changes." Now every schedule change starts as a short written proposal, checked against the records before anyone saves it. In the sim, with DR-1 and its change check, the merge is rejected with its reason; the night peaks at 150 then 190 amps, and the ice holds at -5.0 °C. In November the contractor came back for the winter service, read DR-1 on the proposal form, and left the starts alone.
options.senior: A decision that matters needs its reason kept where the next person meets it: beside the schedule, not in a chat thread. An architecture decision record does that in one page: the context, the decision, and its consequences, including what it costs and when to look again. A record nobody reads is only half the fix, so changes go through a short written proposal checked against the records, the way an RFC is read by others before it is decided. Explaining the trade-off (5 seconds would hold, 2 minutes is margin) lets the next person keep it or undo it on purpose.

options.text: Make the controller refuse any schedule that starts two compressors within 60 seconds.
options.verdict: Trade-off: a rule without its reason
options.part2: The controller's maker added a guard in November: it refuses any schedule with two compressor starts within 60 seconds. In the sim the merge is refused, two starts within 60 seconds, with no reason given; Tamsworth's schedule stays, the night peaks at 150 then 190 amps, and the ice holds at -5.0 °C. In February a new manager asked why the guard was there. Nobody could say; the maker's notes said only "requested by the rink". The guard stays, a rule nobody can explain, and the next unwritten reason in the plant room still has nowhere to live.
options.senior: The guard is honest engineering: it stops this exact mistake every time, without anyone reading anything. But it stops it without saying why, so the next person meets a rule they can't explain, and the reason is still in no one's hands. The next unwritten decision, another gap, setting or limit, has no guard and nowhere to be written. Guards are worth adding after the decision is written down: the record says why, and the guard enforces it.

sim.title: Replay the plant room on 15 October
sim.lede: You're Hjordis, replaying Thursday 15 October 2026 from 02:58:00. As given data: the plant room's main fuse is 200 amps, and it blows once the draw has stayed above its rating for a full second, so a draw over it in one second blows it the next. The lights and pumps draw 30 amps at night. Each compressor draws 120 amps for its first 5 seconds and 40 while it runs. Both rest from 01:00 to 03:00 while the pumps hold the ice at -5.0 °C. Before this evening the schedule started A at 03:00:00 and B at 03:02:00; you can try B at 03:00:03, 03:00:05 or 03:01:00 instead. This evening's tidy moves B to A's time. With the fuse holding, the ice stays at -5.0 °C; with it blown, compressors and pumps stop and the ice warms steadily, 4 °C in 90 minutes from 03:00, read every 10 minutes. The alarm texts the night phone when the ice reaches -1 °C. A guard in the controller can refuse any schedule change with two starts within 60 seconds. The decision record DR-1 says: never start both within 2 minutes: 120-amp starts, 200-amp fuse. It can be absent, pinned beside the schedule, or pinned with every change checked against it. A 300-amp fuse is the supplier's call, not the rink's. Play second by second to 03:05:00, then the ice to 04:30.
sim.tryThis: Try this: play as built: 270 at 03:00:00, the fuse blown at 03:00:01, and the alarm at 04:30, ice -1.0 °C. Turn this evening's tidy off: 150 amps at 03:00:00, peak 190 at 03:02:00, fuse intact. Set B to 03:00:03: the fuse blows at 03:00:04; at 03:00:05 the peak is 190 at 03:00:05 and it holds, so any gap of 5 seconds or more holds. Turn the tidy back on and set the guard: REFUSED by the controller guard, reason none given. Pin DR-1 without the check: the tidy is saved, not checked against DR-1, and the fuse still blows at 03:00:01. Add the check: REJECTED by the change check, with DR-1's reason, and the ice holds at -5.0 °C. Try the 300-amp fuse: 270 at 03:00:00, and it holds.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the compressors broke. Since January 2024, starting B 2 minutes after A had kept the plant room under its 200-amp main fuse. The reason lived only in a chat thread, switched off in June, so on Wednesday evening a contractor merged the starts; at 03:00:00 they drew 120 + 120 + 30 = 270 amps, and the fuse blew at 03:00:01, in a building nobody was watching.

steps.title: Two starts, one fuse.
steps.text: A compressor start, in steps: the motor pulls 120 amps for 5 seconds while it gets up to speed; then it settles at 40 amps; the main fuse sees the sum of everything in the plant room, including the 30 amps of lights and pumps. Tamsworth's schedule: at 03:00:00 A starts, 120 + 30 = 150; at 03:02:00 B starts, 40 + 120 + 30 = 190; both under 200. Merged: 120 + 120 + 30 = 270 at 03:00:00, and a fuse rated 200 blows once the draw has stayed above it for a full second, at 03:00:01. What can go wrong at each step: the start lasts 5 seconds, so nobody sees the peak; the fuse is in another building, so nobody sees it blow; and the controller only sends start signals, so its log says both started. Only the ice told anyone, warming 4 °C in 90 minutes, at 04:30.

steps.title: A decision with its reason missing.
steps.text: The 2-minute gap was a decision. Tamsworth made it in January 2024, the night the new compressors blew the fuse, and wrote the reason in the staff chat. The chat tool was switched off in June with its history, and from then the schedule held the decision but not the reason. Michael Nygard describes exactly this: a new person facing a past decision without its reasons can only blindly accept it or blindly change it. The contractor looked, found no reason and changed it; nothing beside the schedule said otherwise. And the reason would have told him more than "keep the gap": a gap of 5 seconds already holds (in the sim, B at 03:00:05 peaks at 190), so 2 minutes is margin, a judgement rather than a law. Without the reason written down, nobody can tell which part of a number matters.

steps.title: Three ways to write a decision down.
steps.text: A design doc, written before a bigger change, in steps: state the problem and its context; list the goals and the non-goals; describe the design; list the alternatives considered and why each lost; record the trade-offs and the choice. An RFC, short for request for comments, in steps: write the proposal; share it with the people it affects; they comment for a set time; then it is decided, and the outcome is written on it. An architecture decision record, or ADR, for one decision, in steps: a short title; the context, the forces at play; the decision, in full sentences; its consequences, good and bad; a status, and when a later record replaces it, the old one is marked superseded, never deleted. Blueprints made the same move for machines: the code was the drawing the building had to match, and an ADR is the note in its margin saying why a wall is where it is. The Night the Lights Went Out kept the night's steps in a runbook; a decision record keeps the reasons behind them. LATENT's a9e05, Writing It Down, covers writing for a client; this case is writing for the next engineer.

steps.title: The fix, and why the others fall short.
steps.text: DR-1 goes beside the schedule, in ADR shape: the decision, never start both compressors within 2 minutes; the context, 120-amp starts, a 30-amp night load and a 200-amp fuse; the consequences, B starts 2 minutes later, 5 seconds would hold, and it needs another look if the fuse or the load changes. A schedule change then goes in steps: write a short proposal saying what and why; check it against the decision records; if it breaks one, change the plan or write a new record that replaces the old one on purpose; then save. Explaining a trade-off means saying what the choice buys, what it costs and when it stops being true, so the next person can keep it or undo it on purpose. The others fall short: banning contractors leaves the reason in nobody's hands, and staff tidy too; a bigger fuse is the supplier's call and hides the reason; a guard in the controller stops this one merge but says nothing about why, or about the next decision; and recording every meeting buries one reason in hours nobody replays.

steps.title: The walk into the plant room.
steps.text: Writing it down is staff work because the cause is usually in a building you can't see. Everything in the rink building was fine that night: the office lit, the controller showing both compressors started, the thermometer in the ice reporting faithfully. The decision lived in a chat tool that had been switched off in June, and its effect lived in the plant room across the yard, where nothing reports anything. At 04:30, with the alarm on her phone, Hjordis took a torch, crossed the yard and opened the door on a dark, silent room: no hum, no pumps, and on the wall the sealed fuse box, guarding a reason nobody had written down.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for the next tidy. A proposed change, B to 03:00:00, is sent to the change check, which reads decision record DR-1, never both within 2 minutes, before anything is saved. Changes that pass go to the controller, which keeps B 2 minutes after A, and it starts the compressors in the plant room, which peaks at 190 amps under its 200-amp fuse. Below: DR-1 feeds the check, and tonight's merge is rejected with its reason.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the next tidy. A schedule change starts as a short proposal, and the change check reads it against DR-1 before anything is saved. Tonight's merge, both at 03:00:00, breaks DR-1 and is rejected with its reason: 120-amp starts, 200-amp fuse. The controller keeps B 2 minutes after A, and the plant room peaks at 190 amps under its 200-amp fuse.

fix.title: The fix: write the decision down beside the schedule, and check every change against it
fix.text: Write DR-1 as an architecture decision record and keep it where the schedule is changed: pinned beside the controller and copied into the schedule's notes. Title: never start both compressors within 2 minutes. Context: each start draws 120 amps for 5 seconds, the lights and pumps draw 30 at night, and the plant room's main fuse is 200 amps. Decision: B starts 2 minutes after A. Consequences: B starts later; a gap of 5 seconds would hold, so 2 minutes is margin; look again if the fuse or the night load changes. Then make every schedule change start as a short written proposal that is checked against the decision records before it is saved, with one named owner for the check. Write the next decision the same way the day it is made, not after it is lost.

limits: A record only helps while it is true. If the supplier changes the fuse or a new machine joins the plant room's supply, DR-1's context has changed, and it must be replaced on purpose by a new record, not left to go stale or deleted.

A change check is a small step that people skip on a busy night. It needs a named owner and has to sit where changes happen, in the schedule's notes and on the proposal form, not in a folder nobody opens.

Writing things down does not watch the plant room. Nothing there reports a blown fuse; an alarm on the plant room's own power would have warned at 03:00:01 instead of 04:30, and is worth adding alongside the record.

explain.seniorTake: Systems keep their decisions longer than people keep their reasons. Write the reason where the next person will meet it, at the moment they are about to change the thing: one short record per decision with its context, the decision and its consequences; a design doc when a change is big enough to weigh alternatives; a written proposal that others comment on before a shared thing changes. Say what each trade-off buys, what it costs and when it stops being true, so it can be kept or undone on purpose. Guards and bigger limits are fine additions, but only after the reason is written; without it, each is one more rule nobody can explain.

realWorld.title: Design Docs at Google: write down the trade-offs
realWorld.text: Malte Ubl writes that a design doc "documents the high level implementation strategy and key design decisions", and that "The design doc is the place to write down the trade-offs you made in designing your software." He adds: "Focus on those trade-offs to produce a useful document with long-term value." Tamsworth's 2 minutes was such a trade-off: a later start bought a fuse that holds.

realWorld.title: Design Docs at Google: alternatives considered
realWorld.text: One of the sections Ubl lists is "Alternatives considered", which opens: "This section lists alternative designs that would have reasonably achieved similar outcomes." He writes that "this section is one of the most important ones as it shows very explicitly why the selected solution is the best". For the rink, the alternatives were starting together on a bigger fuse, or a gap of a few seconds.

realWorld.title: Design Docs at Google: memory and comment threads
realWorld.text: Among the reasons Ubl gives for design docs: "Form the basis of an organizational memory around design decisions." In review, "Discussion then primarily happens in comment threads in the document." The comments live in the document itself, so they outlast any chat tool.

realWorld.title: Amazon, 2017 Letter to Shareholders: six-page memos
realWorld.text: Jeff Bezos writes: "We don’t do PowerPoint (or any other slide-oriented) presentations at Amazon." and "Instead, we write narratively structured six-page memos." Good memos, he says, are "shared with colleagues who are asked to improve the work". Written as sentences, a memo carries its reasons with it, which a bullet point on a slide usually leaves out.

realWorld.title: Michael Nygard, 2011: blindly accept or blindly change
realWorld.text: Nygard opens: "One of the hardest things to track during the life of a project is the motivation behind certain decisions." A newcomer, "Without understanding the rationale or consequences, this person has only two choices:" "Blindly accept the decision." or "Blindly change it." The contractor's note, no reason found, is the second.

realWorld.title: Michael Nygard: what a decision record holds
realWorld.text: "An architecture decision record is a short text file in a format similar to an Alexandrian pattern." Its context "describes the forces at play, including technological, political, social, and project local"; its consequences section "describes the resulting context, after applying the decision." "The whole document should be one or two pages long." And: "If a decision is reversed, we will keep the old one around, but mark it as superseded."

asked: How do you write a design doc?
What is an architecture decision record, and when do you write one?
How do you explain a trade-off to someone who will inherit the system?
interview.answer: I start from the size of the decision. For a change big enough to weigh options, a design doc: the problem and context, goals and non-goals, the design, the alternatives considered and why each lost, and the trade-offs behind the choice; Malte Ubl calls writing down the trade-offs the point of the document. If the change affects other people or teams, it goes out as an RFC, a written proposal they comment on for a set time before it is decided, with the outcome written on it. For one decision that somebody will one day want to undo, an architecture decision record: one page with the context, the decision and its consequences, kept in the repository beside what it governs, and marked superseded rather than deleted when a later record replaces it. I write one the day the decision is made, especially when the setting looks odd without its reason. To explain a trade-off to whoever inherits the system, I write what the choice buys, what it costs, the numbers behind it and when it stops being true, so they can keep it or undo it on purpose instead of blindly. I'd tell the story of an ice rink whose two compressors started 2 minutes apart for a reason kept only in a chat thread: when the chat tool was switched off and a contractor merged the starts, they drew 270 amps against a 200-amp fuse, and the ice was soft by morning.

atWork: Find one setting in your systems whose reason nobody on the team can give: a waiting time, a limit on tries, a gap between two nightly jobs, a size cap. A reason that lived only in a chat thread and went with the tool is a common pattern: the decision stays in the system, and the why disappears with the history or the person. For each such setting, ask three things. Can someone find its reason where the setting is changed: beside it in the code's repository, in its Terraform or CloudFormation file, on the change form, not in chat? Does a change to it start as a short written proposal that is checked against the decision records? And does the record say what the choice costs and when to look again? Keep the records as short ADRs in the same repository as the code they explain; Nygard's own suggestion is a doc/arch folder. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO 9001:2015, clause 7.5 (documented information) sets requirements for handling documents and records; if it is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, control A.5.37 (documented operating procedures) and control A.8.32 (change management: the details of changes stated and documented) apply; if it is pursuing SOC 2, criterion CC8.1 expects changes to be authorised, documented, tested and approved. A decision record that sits beside the setting, and a change check that reads it, are the evidence those audits look for, so build them in from the first draft rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your team's payment system waits 45 seconds between two nightly jobs. A new engineer wants to cut the wait to zero so the night finishes sooner. Nobody remembers its purpose: the engineer who set it left last year and explained it in a chat channel that has since been deleted. What do you do now, and what would you change so the next setting like this keeps its reason?

keyIdeas.idea: Don't blindly change it or blindly keep it: find or rebuild the reason first
Write it as a decision record (context, decision, consequences) kept beside the setting, not in chat
Make changes start as a short written proposal checked against the records, so the next change meets the reason

recall.model: Don't blindly change it or blindly keep it. First find out why the wait is there: ask around, read old notes, or test what the second job does when it starts early, and rebuild the reason. Then write it as a decision record: the context (what the gap protects), the decision, and the consequences, including what it costs and when to look again, kept in the repository beside the setting, not in chat. Finally, make any change to that setting start as a short written proposal, an RFC for small things, that is checked against the decision records before it is merged, so the next engineer meets the reason before they change the number.

recall.prompt: In the sim, with this evening's tidy on and everything else as built, which one setting stops the merge and also tells the next person why?
options: Controller guard: refuse two starts within 60 seconds
DR-1, and every change checked against it
recall.why: With the change check, the merge is REJECTED and the reason shown is DR-1's: never start both within 2 minutes: 120-amp starts, 200-amp fuse. The guard also stops it, but its reason reads none given. DR-1 pinned up but unchecked lets the merge through, and the fuse blows at 03:00:01. The 300-amp fuse lets the merge run at 270 amps and explains nothing.

recall.prompt: Besides a title and a status, which sections make up Michael Nygard's architecture decision record?
recall.why: Nygard's record has a title, the context (the forces at play), the decision, a status and the consequences (the resulting context after the decision). Goals and non-goals belong to a design doc; summary, timeline and action items to an incident write-up.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: how do you write a design doc, and when would you write an architecture decision record or an RFC instead?

keyIdeas.idea: A design doc covers the problem and context, goals and non-goals, the design, the alternatives considered and the trade-offs behind the choice
An RFC is a written proposal that others comment on before it is decided
An ADR records one decision with its context and consequences, kept with the code and superseded rather than deleted

recall.model: A design doc is for a change big enough to weigh options. I write the problem and its context, the goals and non-goals, the design itself, the alternatives considered with why each lost, and the trade-offs behind the choice, so a reader a year later can see what was given up. An RFC is the step where that proposal goes to the people it affects: they comment on it for a set time before it is decided, and the outcome is written on it. An architecture decision record is smaller: one decision in one page, with its context, the decision and its consequences, kept in the repository next to the code, and marked superseded rather than deleted when a later decision replaces it. When a decision will outlive its author, the ADR is what the next person reads before changing it.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. DR-1 has stood beside the schedule since October, every schedule change has started as a short written proposal, and the contractor's winter service passed without a merge. In January the electricity supplier renewed the plant room's cable and fitted a 300-amp main fuse, its own call. In March the new rink manager asked to start both compressors together after events, so the ice cools sooner, and wants DR-1 deleted: "it says 200 amps, and that isn't true any more." With the new fuse, both starts together draw 270 amps, under 300.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Should DR-1 be deleted, and should the starts be merged?

keyIdeas.idea: Don't delete DR-1: write a new record that supersedes it and mark the old one superseded, so the history of why survives
Redo the sums with the new context: 270 against 300 holds, but with only 30 amps of margin that anything new on the supply would use up
Write down the consequences, what the choice costs and when to look again, so the next person can keep or undo it on purpose

coldCase.model: Don't delete DR-1; its context changed, so the decision needs making again, on purpose. Write a new record, DR-2, that supersedes it, and mark DR-1 superseded rather than deleting it, so the next person can see why the starts were apart and why that changed. Redo the sums: 120 + 120 + 30 = 270 against the new 300-amp fuse holds, but with only 30 amps to spare, and any new machine on the plant room's supply would use that margin up without anyone noticing. So DR-2 should write that margin into its consequences, say what the choice costs and when to look again (any new load in the plant room, any change of fuse), and keep a small gap anyway, since 5 seconds apart peaks at 190 amps and costs almost nothing.
